items: Carl Wilhelm Scheele had made it earlier (1771-1772) but published later; Lavoisier named it and explained its role in burning.
Priestley made oxygen by heating mercuric oxide on 1 August 1774.

Elisha Gray filed a caveat for a similar telephone at the patent office on the same day as Bell's application (14 February 1876); Antonio Meucci had demonstrated a 'telettrofono' and filed a caveat in 1871 but could not renew it.
Bell was granted US patent 174,465 on 7 March 1876 and made the first call to his assistant Thomas Watson in Boston three days later.
Thomson showed in 1897 that cathode rays are made of particles far lighter than atoms.
Berners-Lee proposed a hypertext information system at CERN in March 1989; the first web server ran there in 1990.
The Curies announced polonium in July and radium in December 1898, found in pitchblende.
place: Murray Hill, New Jersey (Bell Labs)
John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley
The point-contact transistor was first shown working at Bell Labs on 16 December 1947.
Einstein, then a patent clerk in Bern, published 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies' in 1905, his 'miracle year'.
Maiman built the first working laser, a ruby laser, in May 1960.
Fleming noticed in September 1928 that a Penicillium mould killed the bacteria around it; Florey and Chain's team in Oxford made it a usable drug from 1940.
Joseph Swan made working carbon lamps in Newcastle at the same time; the two later merged their British companies as Ediswan.
Edison's team made a carbon-filament lamp that burned for hours in October 1879 and showed it publicly at Menlo Park that December.
Nobel stabilised nitroglycerine in kieselguhr at his factory in Krümmel near Hamburg and patented the result as dynamite in 1867.
French soldiers found the stone in July 1799; its Greek text was the key Champollion used to read hieroglyphs in 1822.
Robert Noyce at Fairchild made the first practical silicon (planar) integrated circuit in 1959.
Kilby showed the first working integrated circuit on 12 September 1958.
CERN announced on 4 July 2012 that the Large Hadron Collider had found the particle predicted by Higgs and others in 1964.
Torricelli's mercury tube of 1643 showed that air has weight and measured its pressure.
Pasteur showed in 1864 that gentle heating kept wine from spoiling by killing microbes.
Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish
Bell Burnell noticed the regular radio pulses of the first pulsar in November 1967.
Joseph Henry found the same effect independently in the United States.
Faraday showed in August 1831 that a changing magnetic field makes an electric current, the principle of the dynamo.
Movable type itself was older: Bi Sheng's ceramic type in Song China (about 1040) and metal type in Goryeo Korea (Jikji, 1377).
Gutenberg combined metal movable type, oil-based ink and a screw press in Mainz around 1450; his Bible was finished by about 1455.
Diesel's compression-ignition engine (patented 1893) first ran efficiently at the Augsburg machine works in 1897.
Edison's tinfoil phonograph, the first machine to record and play back sound, was built in late 1877.
Lightning rod and the kite experiment
Franklin's kite experiment of 1752 supported his claim that lightning is electricity, and he promoted lightning rods.
Georges Lemaître had published the relation in 1927.
Hubble showed in 1929 that the farther a galaxy is, the faster it moves away.
The first message between two ARPANET computers went from UCLA to Stanford Research Institute on 29 October 1969.
The French Academy of Sciences announced Daguerre's process in January 1839; it was the first practical photography.
Baekeland made the first fully synthetic plastic in 1907.
Volta described the first electric battery, a stack of zinc and copper discs, in a letter to the Royal Society in 1800.
Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656, making clocks accurate to about a minute a day.
Whitney's gin (1793, patented 1794) separated cotton fibre from seed quickly, making short-staple cotton profitable and spreading slavery in the American South.
Jenner inoculated James Phipps with cowpox in May 1796 and showed that it protected him from smallpox.
Cooke and Wheatstone had patented a working electrical telegraph in Britain in 1837.
Morse sent 'What hath God wrought' from the Capitol in Washington to Baltimore on 24 May 1844.
LIGO detected waves from two merging black holes on 14 September 2015, as Einstein's theory predicted.
The first known working steam engine pumped water from a coal mine near Dudley Castle in 1712.
Hargreaves' multi-spindle spinning frame (about 1764) let one worker spin eight or more threads at once.
Watt's separate condenser (patented 1769) cut the fuel a steam engine needed; the first Boulton and Watt engines went to work in 1776.
Röntgen found the new rays on 8 November 1895 and published in December, with an X-ray of his wife's hand.
place: Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina
On 17 December 1903 the Wright Flyer made four controlled, powered flights, the longest 260 m in 59 seconds.
Archaeology has found older paper in China (2nd century BC); Cai Lun improved and standardised the process.
The court official Cai Lun presented a paper made of bark, hemp and rags to the Han emperor in 105.
The spectacle-maker Lipperhey applied for a patent on a telescope in The Hague in October 1608; it was refused because others made them too.
Einstein presented the field equations of general relativity to the Prussian Academy in Berlin in November 1915.
Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid
Their model rested on X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins at King's College London, published in the same issue.
Watson and Crick published the double helix in Nature in April 1953.
The first artificial satellite was launched on 4 October 1957 and orbited for three weeks of radio signals.
Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, in exile, explained it as the splitting of the nucleus in early 1939.
Hahn and Strassmann found barium among the products of uranium bombarded with neutrons in December 1938.
Banting and Best isolated insulin at the University of Toronto in 1921; the first patient was treated in January 1922.
Benz built his three-wheeled petrol car in 1885 and patented it in January 1886; Bertha Benz drove it to Pforzheim in 1888.
Gunpowder itself was found by Chinese alchemists earlier, probably in the 9th century.
The military manual Wujing Zongyao, compiled for the Song court, gives the earliest known formulas for gunpowder.
Trevithick's locomotive hauled 10 tons of iron and 70 men along the Penydarren tramway on 21 February 1804.
Rocket won the Rainhill Trials of October 1829 and set the pattern of later steam locomotives.
View from the Window at Le Gras
Niépce's 'View from the Window at Le Gras' (1826 or 1827) is the oldest surviving camera photograph.
Many contributed: Hertz (radio waves, 1886-1888), Lodge, Popov, Bose and Tesla.
Marconi sent wireless signals over more than a kilometre at his family's estate in 1895, then patented his system in Britain in 1896.
With his own telescope Galileo saw four moons circling Jupiter in January 1610 and published them in Sidereus Nuncius that March.
Copernicus, a canon of Frombork, put the Sun at the centre of the planets' orbits in De revolutionibus, printed in Nuremberg in 1543.
Newton's laws of motion and gravitation
Newton's Principia (1687) set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
Darwin published On the Origin of Species in November 1859, a year after he and Alfred Russel Wallace presented the theory jointly.
Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic weight in 1869 and left gaps for elements not yet found.
Pasteur's team gave the vaccine to nine-year-old Joseph Meister, bitten by a rabid dog, in July 1885; he survived.
Becquerel found in 1896 that uranium salts fogged photographic plates without light.
Kay's flying shuttle (1733) doubled a weaver's output.
Montgolfier brothers; Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes
On 21 November 1783 a Montgolfier hot-air balloon carried two men over Paris for about 25 minutes.
Fulton's steamboat ran from New York to Albany up the Hudson in August 1807, starting the first commercial steamboat service.
Morton anaesthetised a patient with ether for an operation in public on 16 October 1846.
Otto built the first practical four-stroke internal combustion engine in 1876.
place: Paris (Salon Indien du Grand Café)
The Lumières showed ten short films to a paying audience in Paris on 28 December 1895.
Baird gave the first public demonstration of moving television images in his Soho laboratory on 26 January 1926.
Hans von Ohain and Erich Warsitz
Frank Whittle in Britain had run a jet engine on a test bench in 1937.
The He 178 made the first flight of a turbojet aircraft on 27 August 1939.
John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert
ENIAC, the first programmable general-purpose electronic computer, was completed in late 1945 and unveiled in February 1946.
place: Jornada del Muerto, New Mexico
The Manhattan Project exploded the first atomic bomb on 16 July 1945.
Salk's inactivated vaccine, developed at the University of Pittsburgh, was declared safe and effective on 12 April 1955 after a field trial of 1.8 million children.
Gagarin orbited the Earth once on 12 April 1961.
Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins
Armstrong and Aldrin landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969 and walked on it for about two and a half hours.
Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, Masatoshi Shima
The Intel 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, went on sale in November 1971.
Bayer chemists made pure acetylsalicylic acid in 1897 and sold it as Aspirin from 1899.
Lister published his results with carbolic acid in 1867, sharply cutting deaths after surgery.
Landsteiner described the blood groups in 1901, which made safe transfusion possible.
Planck's law of black-body radiation (December 1900) assumed that energy comes in quanta, the start of quantum physics.
With his own microscopes Leeuwenhoek described bacteria and other 'animalcules' to the Royal Society in 1676.
Harvey showed in De Motu Cordis (1628) that the heart pumps blood round the body in a circuit.
Napier published his tables of logarithms in 1614, which made long calculations in astronomy and navigation far quicker.
Rules for zero and negative numbers (Brahmagupta)
Brahmagupta's treatise of 628 gives the first written rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers.
The Song government took over the merchants' paper notes of Sichuan and issued the first government paper money in 1024.
The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing
Al-Khwarizmi's book on 'completion and balancing' (al-jabr), written in Baghdad around 820, gave algebra its name.
Ibn al-Haytham showed by experiment that we see by light entering the eye; written in Cairo between 1011 and 1021.
The librarian of Alexandria measured the Earth's circumference from the Sun's angle at Syene and Alexandria, around 240 BC.
Zhang Heng presented a seismoscope to the Han court in 132 that showed the direction of a distant earthquake.
Norse Greenlanders had reached Newfoundland about 1000 (L'Anse aux Meadows).
Sailing for Castile, Columbus landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492, beginning lasting European contact with the Americas.
Sea route to India (Vasco da Gama)
Da Gama sailed round Africa and reached Calicut in May 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to India.
Ferdinand Magellan and Juan Sebastián Elcano
Of five ships that left Spain in 1519, one returned in September 1522 under Elcano, having sailed round the world; Magellan was killed in the Philippines.
Cook charted the east coast of Australia in 1770 and claimed it for Britain.
Herschel saw Uranus from his garden in Bath on 13 March 1781, the first planet found with a telescope.
Johann Galle, from Urbain Le Verrier's prediction
John Couch Adams in Cambridge had made a similar prediction.
Galle found Neptune at the Berlin Observatory on 23 September 1846, within a degree of where Le Verrier had calculated it.
The friar Mendel presented his pea-plant experiments in Brno in 1865; they were ignored until 1900.
Koch announced on 24 March 1882 that a bacterium causes tuberculosis.
Carter found the nearly intact tomb in November 1922.
Goddard launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket on 16 March 1926; it flew 12 m high.
Haber made ammonia from the nitrogen of the air in 1909; Carl Bosch scaled it up for fertiliser and explosives.
Discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation
Penzias and Wilson found an unexplained microwave hiss from every direction in 1964, the afterglow of the Big Bang.
Barnard transplanted a heart into Louis Washkansky on 3 December 1967; he lived 18 days.
Louise Brown, the first baby conceived by in vitro fertilisation, was born on 25 July 1978.
Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was born on 5 July 1996.
